original_title: The Devil's Mouth is shark weak

en.title: The Devil's Mouth Drowns in Dullness: Shark Week's Latest Miss
en.summary: This year's Shark Week offering, **The Devil's Mouth**, fails to make a splash, delivering a predictable creature feature that even its cast seems to endure. Director **Jeff Wadlow** returns to genre filmmaking with a film that feels more like a financed vacation than a thrilling horror experience.
en.body:
Director **Jeff Wadlow**, known for his previous foray into genre-bending with the tropical horror of **Fantasy Island**, is back with **The Devil's Mouth** for this year's Shark Week. Unfortunately, his latest straight-to-Amazon film feels less like a thrilling aquatic adventure and more like an extended paid vacation for its cast. The premise, a group of college students trapped in a submerged cave system with a CGI shark, certainly had potential, even earning a spot on the Black List in 2019 for its script by **Aja Gabel** and **Myung Joh Wesner**. However, the execution proves to be as lifeless as the characters themselves.

Instead of a tense survival thriller, audiences are subjected to a film where the primary source of dread seems to be the boredom shared by the actors. Much like the real-life drama of **Thirteen Lives**, the characters are confined to a dark, muddy, flooded environment, but without the stakes or emotional resonance. The underwater labyrinth becomes a monotonous backdrop for a series of uninspired encounters with an unconvincingly animated bull shark. The ensemble cast, a collection of archetypal college students, appear utterly disengaged from their dire predicament, delivering lines with a flatness that suggests they are as eager for rescue as the audience is for the credits to roll. Even a moment meant to establish character, like **Kathryn Newton**'s **Sara** declaring, "I just accepted that job," feels more like an actor reciting a line than a character grappling with survival.

## A Sinking Premise

**The Devil's Mouth** squanders its initial promise by focusing on tedious exposition and a lack of genuine peril. The claustrophobic setting, which should have been a breeding ground for suspense and terror, is rendered inert by **Wadlow**'s uninspired direction. The CGI creature, a crucial element for any effective creature feature, is disappointingly rendered, further detracting from any semblance of fear. The film mistakes confinement for tension, failing to build any meaningful connection between the audience and the characters, thereby neutralizing the impact of their potential demise. It’s a missed opportunity to explore the psychological toll of being trapped, opting instead for a superficial slasher-lite approach that doesn’t even commit to its own genre.

## Fan Disappointment and What It Means

For fans eagerly anticipating a Shark Week movie that breaks the mold, **The Devil's Mouth** delivers a familiar disappointment. The film's reliance on tired tropes and weak character development leaves little room for audience investment. Viewers who tune in for thrilling shark encounters or compelling survival narratives will likely find themselves adrift in a sea of mediocrity. The film's failure to capitalize on its intriguing premise or deliver a satisfying genre experience reflects a broader trend of uninspired direct-to-streaming horror that prioritizes production convenience over genuine entertainment value. This lack of innovation is particularly frustrating for dedicated fans who crave fresh takes on familiar concepts.

## What's Next

Details regarding future projects from director **Jeff Wadlow** or any potential follow-ups to **The Devil's Mouth** have not yet been announced. For those seeking a more satisfying aquatic thriller, exploring films like **The Shallows** or **47 Meters Down** might prove more rewarding.

content_raw: Back in 2020, director Jeff Wadlow blazed a boring trail for destination vacations masquerading as feature films. Where most of those movies are either rom-coms subsidized by the tourism board of wherever they’re set, or Adam Sandler comedies filled with people he’d be hanging out with off-camera anyways, Fantasy Island took horror to the tropics. It was terrible, but at least it was a mix of genre and locale we don’t often get. For this year’s Shark Week, the purveyor of Blumhouse schlock like Truth Or Dare and Imaginary makes his first straight-to-Amazon film, The Devil’s Mouth , which once again has more to offer its cast (a financed getaway) than its audience (a boring CGI creature feature). Yet, because of the particulars of the plot, even the actors probably didn’t have too much fun with this thing. They seem to have spent most of their time like the stranded soccer team dramatized in Thirteen Lives : stuck in a dark, muddy, flooded Thai cave awaiting rescue. But the only thing coming for this ensemble—a slasher’s worth of hot-blooded (or at least blood-filled) undergrads—is an unconvincingly animated bull shark stuck in the same submerged cave system. It’s a claustrophobic premise, one that earned Aja Gabel and Myung Joh Wesner’s script a place on the Black List back in 2019, sunk like an anchor by its limp characters and Wadlow’s lifeless filmmaking. It should be fun watching this friend group get torn apart in this aquatic labyrinth, but the characters seem disinterested not only in their predicament but in their own barely written lives. “I just accepted that job,” declares Kathryn Newton’s responsible Sara in a moment of character-establishing conversation, “the one I worked really hard to get.” Sara—aside from being the only one with a brain in her head—is the single one of the group, which means she’s going to be the survivor; the others are coupled up: overbearing party girl Max (Lana Condor) and the gormless James (Nico Hiraga), and the vapid lovebirds Greg (Gavin Casalegno) and Adrienne (Tommi Rose). Though Max finds some specificity in being Sara’s BFF, with some of the intimate contentiousness that implies, the rest of the group splits a single personality between them. They all speak in the same dialect of embarrassing quips and blunt exposition, volume making up for substance. The poor shark must feel like it’s opened a bag of chips, only to find that it’s mostly air inside. The tourists head towards their cavebound doom guided by local Wat ( White Lotus ‘ Tayme Thapthimthong), whom they immediately overrule in order to take the more difficult path through The Devil’s Mouth.
